docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This package provides Griffe extensions that help mkdocstrings understand some helpers from frequenz-core.

Some of these helpers use patterns that Griffe can't fully understand by just reading the source code. This means that some information might be missing from the generated API documentation.

The extensions fill in these gaps. The first one handles deprecations: frequenz-core can deprecate APIs using function calls instead of decorators. Neither Griffe's built-in support for @deprecated nor griffe-warnings-deprecated can detect these calls.

The extensions recognize helpers by their fully qualified names, without importing frequenz-core. So you don't need frequenz-core as a dependency, and you can use the extensions to document any project that uses these helpers.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add griffe-frequenz-core to your documentation dependencies, alongside mkdocstrings.

Then enable the extensions you want in the extensions option of the mkdocstrings Python handler, as shown below.

docs.title: Documenting deprecations
docs.text:
The griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations extension finds deprecations made using frequenz-core helper functions.

It works alongside griffe-warnings-deprecated, which handles deprecations made using decorators. You can enable both:

plugins:
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          options:
            extensions:
              - griffe_warnings_deprecated
              - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations

By default, both extensions use the same format, so all deprecations look the same in your documentation.

For each deprecated object, the extension:

  • Adds a deprecated label.
  • Stores the deprecation notice in the object's deprecated field.
  • Adds an admonition with the notice at the top of its docstring.

The notices follow the deprecations guide.

A warning shown at runtime is different from a notice in the documentation. The runtime warning needs to identify the deprecated object. In the documentation, readers already know which object they're looking at.

So a documentation notice should simply say since which version the object is deprecated and what to use instead, with a link to the replacement.

The extension tries to build this notice from the arguments passed to the helper. If you need a different notice, you can write one yourself using a Deprecated: section in the docstring. A hand-written notice always takes priority.

Sometimes the extension can't get all the information it needs. For example, it might not be able to read an argument from the source code, or the helper might only have the runtime warning. In that case, it still adds a notice with whatever information is available, but also logs a warning. This makes mkdocs build --strict fail, so you can fix the documentation by writing the missing notice yourself.

If you use a different admonition style for deprecations, you can change the kind option. For example:

plugins:
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          options:
            extensions:
              - griffe_warnings_deprecated:
                  kind: deprecated
              - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations:
                  kind: deprecated

docs.title: Recognized frequenz-core helpers
docs.text:
The extension currently understands these helpers:

frequenz-core helper How it's used What gets documented frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases() Assigned to a module's __getattr__ All aliases in the table frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias An entry in that table The alias frequenz.core.enum.deprecated_member() Used as an enum member's value The enum member frequenz.core.enum.DeprecatedMember Used as an enum member's value The enum member

Griffe resolves imports before matching these names, so aliases work too. For example, this is recognized:

from frequenz.core.enum import deprecated_member as dm

docs.title: Deprecated module aliases
docs.text:
When you move or rename something, you might want to keep the old name working for a while.

The deprecated_aliases() helper lets you do this by setting a module's __getattr__. You can also declare the old names under TYPE_CHECKING, so type checkers can still find them.

Each old name is described by a DeprecatedAlias entry. You can provide:

  • new_module: The module where the object lives now.
  • new_name: Its new name, if it was renamed.
  • since: The version where the old name became deprecated.
  • message: A custom runtime warning.

You need to provide new_module, new_name or both. In frequenz-core 1.6.0, since and message are optional. You can pass either, both or neither.

For example:

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, TypeAlias

from frequenz.core.warnings import DeprecatedAlias, deprecated_aliases

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mypkg.newmod import Gadget as _Gadget
    from mypkg.newmod import Widget as _Widget

    Widget: TypeAlias = _Widget
    """A widget that does widget things."""

    Doohickey: TypeAlias = _Gadget
    """A gadget, formerly known as `Doohickey`."""
else:
    __getattr__ = deprecated_aliases(
        __name__,
        DeprecatedAlias("Widget", new_module="mypkg.newmod", since="v1.2.0"),
        DeprecatedAlias(
            "Doohickey", new_module="mypkg.newmod", new_name="Gadget", since="v1.3.0"
        ),
        DeprecatedAlias("Thingamajig", new_name="Widget", since="v1.4.0"),
    )

Suppose this code is in mypkg.oldmod. Here's what happens in the generated documentation:

  • Widget gets the notice "Deprecated since v1.2.0. Use mypkg.newmod.Widget instead." The replacement is linked, and its value is shown as mypkg.newmod.Widget instead of the private _Widget.
  • Doohickey points to mypkg.newmod.Gadget, because both the module and the name changed.
  • Thingamajig points to mypkg.oldmod.Widget, because only the name changed. Its notice says "Use Widget instead.", with a link to that name.

A few other things worth knowing:

  • You don't need a TYPE_CHECKING declaration for every alias. The extension marks all aliases as deprecated. If a name isn't declared under TYPE_CHECKING, it creates a module attribute for it, so the alias still appears in the documentation.
  • You can customize the notice using default_message. The extension replaces {since} with the version string exactly as provided. The notice appears next to the alias in the documentation, so it doesn't repeat the deprecated name. It links the replacement using code formatting.
  • The message argument only affects runtime warnings. It doesn't change the documentation notice. If an entry has no since, the notice only says what to use instead, and the extension logs a warning. To fix this, pass since or write a Deprecated: section in the docstring under TYPE_CHECKING.
  • Replacement links use normal cross-references. If a link can't be resolved, mkdocs-autorefs reports it. For replacements in another project, add that project's objects.inv URL to the Python handler's inventories.
  • Each alias is processed separately. If the extension can't read one entry, it skips that entry and continues with the others. Arguments such as category and stacklevel don't affect the documentation.
  • The helper must be assigned directly to __getattr__. A custom def __getattr__() that calls deprecated_aliases() internally won't be recognized. Neither will a __getattr__ created in some other way.

docs.title: Deprecated enum members
docs.text:
You can deprecate an enum member by wrapping its value with deprecated_member() or DeprecatedMember. In frequenz-core 1.6.0, you can pass new_name to say which member to use instead, and since to say when the member became deprecated. If there is no replacement, pass a runtime message and write the notice by hand.

For example:

from frequenz.core.enum import DeprecatedMember, Enum, deprecated_member


class TaskStatus(Enum):
    OPEN = 1
    PENDING = deprecated_member(1, new_name="OPEN", since="v1.2.0")
    WAITING = DeprecatedMember(1, new_name="OPEN")

    CANCELLED = deprecated_member(
        4,
        "mypkg.TaskStatus.CANCELLED is deprecated. Cancelled tasks are deleted now.",
        since="v1.3.0",
    )
    """The task was cancelled.

    Deprecated:
        Deprecated since v1.3.0. Cancelled tasks are deleted now.
    """

The extension marks all three members and shows their actual value instead of the wrapper. For example, the documentation shows PENDING = 1, not the call to deprecated_member().

Here's how the notices differ:

  • PENDING has new_name and since, so the extension generates its notice using default_message: "Deprecated since v1.2.0. Use OPEN instead." OPEN links to mypkg.TaskStatus.OPEN. The link only shows the member's name, because it's in the same enum.
  • WAITING has new_name but no since. Its notice only says what to use instead, and the extension logs a warning about the missing version.
  • CANCELLED has no new_name, so it needs a hand-written notice. Without one, the extension shows the runtime message as Markdown and logs a warning. Because CANCELLED passes since, that notice would start with "Deprecated since v1.3.0.", followed by the message.

If you pass both new_name and message, the message only changes the runtime warning. The extension still builds the notice from new_name and since.

If an argument comes from a variable or a function call, the extension can't read it. It still marks the member as deprecated and shows its value without the wrapper. Unless you write a notice by hand, it uses the information it can read and logs a warning about anything missing. If it can't read any information for the notice, it uses:

Deprecated. It will be removed in a future release.

docs.title: Hand-written admonitions
docs.text:
Sometimes the generated notice isn't enough. For example, you might want to explain how to migrate to a new API or link to a migration guide.

You can do this by adding a deprecation admonition to the object's docstring.

If the extension finds one, it doesn't add another admonition. It still adds the deprecated label and fills in the deprecated field.

The extension also moves your notice to the top of the docstring, before the summary, so it appears in the same place as a generated notice. You can't write it there yourself, because a docstring must start with its summary.

It recognizes two kinds of hand-written admonitions:

  • A Deprecated: section in the docstring.
  • An admonition whose title matches the extension's title option (case-insensitive).

For example:

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    Widget: TypeAlias = _Widget
    """A widget that does widget things.

    Deprecated:
        Deprecated since v1.2.0. Use [`mypkg.newmod.Widget`][] instead, as
        explained in the [migration guide](https://example.com/migration).
    """

Use a hand-written notice whenever the extension can't generate a complete one, or when you want to give readers more information.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
Griffe reads Python source code without running it. This means the extension can't evaluate variables, call functions, or work out values that are only known at runtime. Sometimes it can still mark an object as deprecated, even if it can't read all the arguments of the call.

Here are the main limitations:

  • Module aliases need literal strings. The alias name, new_module, new_name, and since must be written as string literals in the call. If the alias name isn't a literal, the extension can't mark it as deprecated. If another value isn't a literal, the notice leaves out the information it can't read, and the alias value is only shown as the target if the extension can read the target. The message argument is never read for module aliases.

  • Enum notices need literal strings. The extension can only read new_name, since and message if they're string literals. It reads message only when new_name isn't passed or can't be read. Constants, function calls, f-strings, and strings joined with + aren't evaluated. Adjacent string literals are fine, because Python joins them automatically. If an argument isn't a literal, the member is still marked as deprecated and its value is shown without the wrapper. The notice uses whatever information the extension can read.

  • Alias entries must appear directly in the call. Each entry must be a DeprecatedAlias(...) call inside deprecated_aliases(). Entries stored in variables or unpacked from a collection can't be read. For example, neither of these entries will be marked:

deprecated_aliases(__name__, WIDGET)
deprecated_aliases(__name__, *ALIASES)

  • Arguments can't be unpacked. Calls to deprecated_member(), DeprecatedMember, and DeprecatedAlias must use explicit arguments, not *args or **kwargs. For example, a member defined as deprecated_member(*ARGS) is still marked as deprecated, with a generic message, but its value is shown as the whole call. For aliases, unpacked keyword arguments mean only the alias name can be read. If positional arguments are unpacked, the alias isn't marked at all.

  • The extension doesn't validate your code. It matches arguments the same way Python would when calling the function. If the arguments don't match the function's signature, the call is skipped. But the extension doesn't check whether the argument values are valid. That's a job for your tests, which should catch invalid calls when the module is imported.

All these limitations produce warnings when they affect the generated documentation. This lets mkdocs build --strict catch problems instead of silently generating incomplete documentation.

For example, you'll get a warning if:

  • A notice is missing the deprecation version or replacement.
  • A runtime warning is used as the documentation notice.
  • A deprecated value can't be shown correctly.
  • A deprecation can't be marked at all.

Writing your own deprecation admonition fixes warnings about missing or incomplete notices, but not other problems.

If you want to know why the extension couldn't read something, run mkdocs build --verbose. The extension logs those details at debug level.

Broken links to replacements are reported separately by mkdocs-autorefs.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Effect kind danger The kind of the admonition, which is also its CSS class. title Deprecated The title of the admonition. An empty title or null means no title. label deprecated The label added to deprecated objects. null means no label. alias_table_functions frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases The paths of the functions that create a module __getattr__. alias_classes frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias The paths of the callables that create one alias entry. member_wrapper_functions frequenz.core.enum.deprecated_member, frequenz.core.enum.DeprecatedMember The paths of the callables that wrap a deprecated enum member's value. default_message Deprecated since {since}. Use {new_link} instead. The notice template for aliases and enum members with new_name. See the placeholders below. show_target true Show an alias' value as its target, instead of the private name.

You can use these placeholders in default_message:

  • {old}: The fully qualified path of the deprecated object.
  • {new}: The fully qualified path of its replacement.
  • {new_link}: A link to the replacement in code font. If the replacement is in the same module or enum, the link only shows its name.
  • {since}: The version string, as written in the call.

The three path options are lists. If you set one, it replaces the default. To use your own helper as well as the frequenz-core one, list both:

extensions:
  - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations:
      alias_table_functions:
        - frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases
        - mypkg.compat.moved_to

Your own helpers need to take the same arguments as the frequenz-core helper they replace, because the extension reads their calls the same way:

  • Alias tables work like deprecated_aliases(module, /, *aliases). Every positional argument after the module is an alias entry. Keyword arguments are ignored.
  • Alias entries work like DeprecatedAlias(name, /, *, new_module=None, new_name=None, since=None, message=None). The name is positional, and everything else is passed by keyword. You need to pass new_module, new_name or both. since and message are optional and independent. Passing None is the same as not passing the argument.
  • Enum member wrappers work like deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None, since=None). You can pass the value and message positionally or by keyword. new_name and since must be keyword arguments. You need to pass message, new_name or both. Passing None for an optional argument is the same as not passing it.

If frequenz-core renames or moves a helper, you can update these options with the new path. You don't need to wait for a new release of this package.

There is one difference from griffe-warnings-deprecated, on purpose. If title is empty, griffe-warnings-deprecated puts the message in the admonition title, but this extension doesn't, for two reasons:

  • The notice contains a link to the replacement, which doesn't belong in a title.
  • The extension uses the title to recognize hand-written admonitions.

docs.title: Supported Platforms
docs.text:
The following platforms are officially supported (tested):

  • Python: 3.11
  • Operating System: Ubuntu Linux 20.04
  • Architectures: amd64, arm64

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: If you want to know how to build this project and contribute to it, please check out the Contributing Guide.

docs.title: Contributing to Griffe Extensions for frequenz-core
Build
docs.text:
You can use build to simply build the source and binary distribution:

python -m pip install build
python -m build

docs.title: Local development
docs.text:
You can use editable installs to develop the project locally (it will install all the dependencies too):

python -m pip install -e .

Or you can install all development dependencies (mypy, pylint, pytest, etc.) in one go too: 

python -m pip install -e .[dev]

If you don't want to install all the dependencies, you can also use nox to run the tests and other checks creating its own virtual environments:

python -m pip install .[dev-noxfile]
nox

You can also use nox -R to reuse the current testing environment to speed up test at the expense of a higher chance to end up with a dirty test environment.

docs.title: Running tests / checks individually
docs.text:
For a better development test cycle you can install the runtime and test dependencies and run pytest manually.

python -m pip install .[dev-pytest]  # included in .[dev] too

# And for example
pytest tests/test_*.py

Or you can use nox:

nox -R -s pytest -- tests/test_*.py

The same applies to pylint or mypy for example:

nox -R -s pylint -- tests/test_*.py
nox -R -s mypy -- tests/test_*.py

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
To build the documentation, first install the dependencies (if you didn't install all dev dependencies):

python -m pip install -e .[dev-mkdocs]

Then you can build the documentation (it will be written in the site/ directory):

mkdocs build

Or you can just serve the documentation without building it using:

mkdocs serve

Your site will be updated live when you change your files (provided that you used pip install -e ., beware of a common pitfall of using pip install without -e, in that case the API reference won't change unless you do a new pip install).

To build multi-version documentation, we use mike. If you want to see how the multi-version sites looks like locally, you can use:

mike deploy my-version
mike set-default my-version
mike serve

mike works in mysterious ways. Some basic information:

  • mike deploy will do a mike build and write the results to your local gh-pages branch. my-version is an arbitrary name for the local version you want to preview.
  • mike set-default is needed so when you serve the documentation, it goes to your newly produced documentation by default.
  • mike serve will serve the contents of your local gh-pages branch. Be aware that, unlike mkdocs serve, changes to the sources won't be shown live, as the mike deploy step is needed to refresh them.

Be careful not to use --push with mike deploy, otherwise it will push your local gh-pages branch to the origin remote.

That said, if you want to test the actual website in your fork, you can always use mike deploy --push --remote your-fork-remote, and then access the GitHub pages produced for your fork.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
These are the steps to create a new release:

  1. Get the latest head you want to create a release from.

If you use milestones, check that the milestone for this release has no open issues left, and move whatever won't make it to a later milestone.

  1. Update the RELEASE_NOTES.md file if it is not complete, up to date, and remove template comments (<!-- ... -->) and empty sections. Submit a pull request if an update is needed, wait until it is merged, and update the latest head you want to create a release from to get the new merged pull request.

This can't be left for later: the notes published with the release are read from the RELEASE_NOTES.md committed at the tagged commit, not from the tag message.

  1. Create a new signed tag using the release notes and a semver compatible version number with a v prefix, for example:
git tag -s --cleanup=whitespace -F RELEASE_NOTES.md v0.0.1

The signature is not optional: the Protect released tags ruleset rejects unsigned tags. It also forbids updating or deleting a released tag, so make sure you are tagging the commit you want.

  1. Push the new tag.

  2. A GitHub action will test the tag and if all goes well it will create a GitHub Release, and upload a new package to PyPI automatically.

  3. Once this is done, reset the RELEASE_NOTES.md with the template:

cp .github/RELEASE_NOTES.template.md RELEASE_NOTES.md

Commit the new release notes and create a PR (this step should be automated eventually too).

  1. If you use milestones, close the milestone for this release, and create the next one if it doesn't exist yet.

  2. Celebrate!

docs.title: griffe_frequenz_core
docs.text:
Griffe extensions to help mkdocstrings understand frequenz-core helpers.

Some frequenz-core helpers use patterns that Griffe can't fully understand by just reading the source code. This means that some information might be missing from the generated API documentation. Each extension in this package fills in one of these gaps, and we add new ones when more helpers need it.

The extensions recognize helpers by their fully qualified names, without importing frequenz-core. So this package doesn't depend on frequenz-core, and you can use it to document any project that uses these helpers.

Each extension lives in its own submodule, and you enable it using the submodule's path, for example griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations.

Nothing is re-exported here on purpose. When you enable a module path, Griffe creates every extension class it finds in that module, all with the same options. So if this package re-exported the extensions, enabling it would pass the same options to unrelated extensions as soon as we add a second one.

Available extensions:

  • deprecations: Deprecations made with a function call instead of a decorator.

docs.title: griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations
docs.text:
Document deprecations made with function calls.

Python APIs are usually deprecated with a decorator, and Griffe already supports that. griffe-warnings-deprecated adds an admonition and a label to anything decorated with @warnings.deprecated or @typing_extensions.deprecated.

Some frequenz-core helpers can't use a decorator, so they use a function call instead. Griffe doesn't detect these calls. This module adds support for the two cases frequenz-core has: module aliases and enum members. See DeprecationsExtension for examples and how to enable the extension.

docs.title: griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations.DeprecationsExtension
docs.text:
Bases: Extension

An extension to document deprecations made with frequenz-core helpers.

The extension understands two kinds of calls. For each deprecated object it finds, it does the same as griffe-warnings-deprecated does for decorated objects:

  • Adds a deprecated label.
  • Stores the deprecation notice in the object's deprecated field.
  • Adds an admonition with the notice at the top of its docstring.

The first kind is a table of module aliases, used by a module __getattr__ to keep old names working:

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, TypeAlias

from frequenz.core.warnings import DeprecatedAlias, deprecated_aliases

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mypkg.newmod import Widget as _Widget

    Widget: TypeAlias = _Widget  # plus its usual attribute docstring
else:
    __getattr__ = deprecated_aliases(
        __name__,
        DeprecatedAlias("Widget", new_module="mypkg.newmod", since="v1.2.0"),
    )

The extension marks every alias in the table, even if it isn't declared for type checkers. Its notice is built from default_message, linking its target and saying since which version it is deprecated. since is optional, but without it the notice only says what to use instead, and the extension logs a warning.

If an entry has new_name, the object was also renamed. If it doesn't have new_module, it points to another name in the same module. The entry's message is only used for the runtime warning, and doesn't change the notice. To change the notice, write it by hand.

The second kind is an enum member with a wrapped value:

from frequenz.core.enum import Enum, deprecated_member

class TaskStatus(Enum):
    OPEN = 1
    PENDING = deprecated_member(1, new_name="OPEN", since="v1.2.0")

The extension marks the member and shows its actual value instead of the wrapper call, so the documentation shows PENDING = 1. frequenz-core also accepts DeprecatedMember(1, new_name="OPEN", since="v1.2.0"), and the extension recognizes it too.

If you pass new_name, the extension builds a notice using default_message, just as it does for aliases. The notice says since which version the member is deprecated and links to the replacement. The link only shows the member's name, because it's in the same enum. A message passed with new_name only changes the runtime warning, not the notice.

Without new_name, you should write a Deprecated: section in the member's docstring. Otherwise, the extension shows the runtime warning as the notice. If you pass since, the notice starts with "Deprecated since .", followed by the warning.

If you write a notice by hand, the extension uses it instead of the generated one. It also moves it to the top of the docstring, where a generated notice would go.

Warning

Griffe never runs the code, so the extension can only read string literals written directly in the call. If it can't read something, it still marks the object as deprecated when it can, and leaves the missing information out of the notice:

  • An alias only needs its name to be a string literal to be marked. Its value is only shown as the target if new_module and new_name are string literals.
  • If an enum member's new_name, since or message isn't a literal, the member is still marked. The notice uses whatever information the extension can read. If it can read the message but not new_name, it shows the message, like for a member without new_name. If it can't read any, the notice is "Deprecated. It will be removed in a future release." The value is still shown without the wrapper, for example CANCELLED = 1.
  • If the enum wrapper's arguments are unpacked from *args or **kwargs, the member also gets the generic message. Its value is shown as the whole wrapper call, because the extension can't tell which argument is the value.

The extension can't mark an alias if it can't read its name. This happens when:

  • The entry isn't a DeprecatedAlias(...) call written directly in the deprecated_aliases() call, for example because it's stored in a constant or unpacked from *args.
  • The name isn't a string literal.
  • The positional arguments of the entry are unpacked.
  • The arguments don't match the ones of the runtime helper. The extension doesn't check the argument values, though.

The extension logs a warning in all these cases, so a strict build fails. It also logs a warning if a notice doesn't say since which version the object is deprecated and what to use instead, or if it shows the runtime warning. If you wrote the notice by hand, these warnings about the notice aren't logged. You can see why something couldn't be read with mkdocs -v, which shows the debug logs.

To enable it, add it to the mkdocstrings Python handler, together with griffe-warnings-deprecated:

plugins:
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          options:
            extensions:
              - griffe_warnings_deprecated
              - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations

By default, both extensions use the same format, so all deprecations look the same. You can change this and other settings using options:

            extensions:
              - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations:
                  kind: deprecated
                  alias_table_functions:
                    - frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases
                    - mypkg.compat.moved_to
                  alias_classes:
                    - frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias
                    - mypkg.compat.Moved
Note

The paths of the helpers are options on purpose. If frequenz-core renames a helper, you can update the option with the new path. You don't need to wait for a new release of this package.

Note

There is one difference from griffe-warnings-deprecated, on purpose. If title is empty, griffe-warnings-deprecated puts the message in the admonition title, but this extension doesn't. The notice contains a link to the target, which doesn't belong in a title. The extension also uses the title to find out if a docstring already has its own deprecation admonition. Please don't "fix" this.

Source code in src/griffe_frequenz_core/deprecations.py 
class DeprecationsExtension(Extension):  # pylint: disable=too-many-instance-attributes
    """An extension to document deprecations made with `frequenz-core` helpers.

    The extension understands two kinds of calls. For each deprecated object it
    finds, it does the same as `griffe-warnings-deprecated` does for decorated
    objects:

    - Adds a `deprecated` label.
    - Stores the deprecation notice in the object's `deprecated` field.
    - Adds an admonition with the notice at the top of its docstring.

    The first kind is a table of module aliases, used by a module `__getattr__` to
    keep old names working:

    ```python
    from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, TypeAlias

    from frequenz.core.warnings import DeprecatedAlias, deprecated_aliases

    if TYPE_CHECKING:
        from mypkg.newmod import Widget as _Widget

        Widget: TypeAlias = _Widget  # plus its usual attribute docstring
    else:
        __getattr__ = deprecated_aliases(
            __name__,
            DeprecatedAlias("Widget", new_module="mypkg.newmod", since="v1.2.0"),
        )
    ```

    The extension marks every alias in the table, even if it isn't declared for
    type checkers. Its notice is built from `default_message`, linking its
    target and saying since which version it is deprecated. `since` is optional,
    but without it the notice only says what to use instead, and the extension
    logs a warning.

    If an entry has `new_name`, the object was also renamed. If it doesn't have
    `new_module`, it points to another name in the same module. The entry's
    `message` is only used for the runtime warning, and doesn't change the
    notice. To change the notice, write it by hand.

    The second kind is an enum member with a wrapped value:

    ```python
    from frequenz.core.enum import Enum, deprecated_member

    class TaskStatus(Enum):
        OPEN = 1
        PENDING = deprecated_member(1, new_name="OPEN", since="v1.2.0")
    ```

    The extension marks the member and shows its actual value instead of the
    wrapper call, so the documentation shows `PENDING = 1`. `frequenz-core` also
    accepts `DeprecatedMember(1, new_name="OPEN", since="v1.2.0")`, and the
    extension recognizes it too.

    If you pass `new_name`, the extension builds a notice using `default_message`,
    just as it does for aliases. The notice says since which version the member
    is deprecated and links to the replacement. The link only shows the member's
    name, because it's in the same enum. A `message` passed with `new_name` only
    changes the runtime warning, not the notice.

    Without `new_name`, you should write a `Deprecated:` section in the member's
    docstring. Otherwise, the extension shows the runtime warning as the notice.
    If you pass `since`, the notice starts with "Deprecated since <since>.",
    followed by the warning.

    If you write a notice by hand, the extension uses it instead of the generated
    one. It also moves it to the top of the docstring, where a generated notice
    would go.

    Warning:
        Griffe never runs the code, so the extension can only read string
        literals written directly in the call. If it can't read something, it
        still marks the object as deprecated when it can, and leaves the missing
        information out of the notice:

        - An alias only needs its name to be a string literal to be marked. Its
          value is only shown as the target if `new_module` and `new_name` are
          string literals.
        - If an enum member's `new_name`, `since` or message isn't a literal,
          the member is still marked. The notice uses whatever information the
          extension can read. If it can read the message but not `new_name`, it
          shows the message, like for a member without `new_name`. If it can't
          read any, the notice is "Deprecated. It will be removed in a future
          release." The value is still shown without the wrapper, for example
          `CANCELLED = 1`.
        - If the enum wrapper's arguments are unpacked from `*args` or
          `**kwargs`, the member also gets the generic message. Its value is
          shown as the whole wrapper call, because the extension can't tell
          which argument is the value.

        The extension can't mark an alias if it can't read its name. This
        happens when:

        - The entry isn't a `DeprecatedAlias(...)` call written directly in the
          `deprecated_aliases()` call, for example because it's stored in a
          constant or unpacked from `*args`.
        - The name isn't a string literal.
        - The positional arguments of the entry are unpacked.
        - The arguments don't match the ones of the runtime helper. The
          extension doesn't check the argument values, though.

        The extension logs a warning in all these cases, so a strict build
        fails. It also logs a warning if a notice doesn't say since which
        version the object is deprecated and what to use instead, or if it
        shows the runtime warning. If you wrote the notice by hand, these
        warnings about the notice aren't logged. You can see why something
        couldn't be read with `mkdocs -v`, which shows the debug logs.

    To enable it, add it to the mkdocstrings Python handler, together with
    `griffe-warnings-deprecated`:

    ```yaml
    plugins:
      - mkdocstrings:
          handlers:
            python:
              options:
                extensions:
                  - griffe_warnings_deprecated
                  - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations
    ```

    By default, both extensions use the same format, so all deprecations look the
    same. You can change this and other settings using options:

    ```yaml
                extensions:
                  - griffe_frequenz_core.deprecations:
                      kind: deprecated
                      alias_table_functions:
                        - frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases
                        - mypkg.compat.moved_to
                      alias_classes:
                        - frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias
                        - mypkg.compat.Moved
    ```

    Note:
        The paths of the helpers are options on purpose. If `frequenz-core`
        renames a helper, you can update the option with the new path. You don't
        need to wait for a new release of this package.

    Note:
        There is one difference from `griffe-warnings-deprecated`, on purpose.
        If `title` is empty, `griffe-warnings-deprecated` puts the message in
        the admonition title, but this extension doesn't. The notice contains a
        link to the target, which doesn't belong in a title. The extension also
        uses the title to find out if a docstring already has its own
        deprecation admonition. Please don't "fix" this.
    """

    # Each option is a key in `mkdocs.yml`, so we can't group them.
    def __init__(  # pylint: disable=too-many-arguments
        self,
        kind: str = "danger",
        title: str | None = "Deprecated",
        label: str | None = "deprecated",
        *,
        alias_table_functions: Sequence[str] = (
            "frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases",
        ),
        alias_classes: Sequence[str] = ("frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias",),
        member_wrapper_functions: Sequence[str] = (
            "frequenz.core.enum.deprecated_member",
            "frequenz.core.enum.DeprecatedMember",
        ),
        default_message: str = "Deprecated since {since}. Use {new_link} instead.",
        show_target: bool = True,
    ) -> None:
        """Initialize the extension.

        Args:
            kind: The kind of the admonition added to the docstring.
            title: The title of that admonition. If empty, the admonition has no
                title.
            label: The label added to deprecated objects, or `None` to add no
                label.
            alias_table_functions: The fully qualified paths of the functions that
                create a module `__getattr__` from an alias table. Their calls are
                read as if they were calls to
                `deprecated_aliases(module, /, *aliases)`: every positional
                argument after the module is an alias entry, and keyword
                arguments are ignored.
            alias_classes: The fully qualified paths of the callables that create
                one alias entry. Their calls are read as if they were calls to
                `DeprecatedAlias(name, /, *, new_module=None, new_name=None,
                since=None, message=None)`, with at least one of `new_module` and
                `new_name`. `since` and `message` are optional and independent.
            member_wrapper_functions: The fully qualified paths of the callables
                that wrap an enum member's value to deprecate it. They can be
                classes or functions, because calling them looks the same. Their
                calls are read as if they were calls to
                `deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None,
                since=None)`. At least one of `message` and `new_name` is required.
            default_message: The template for notices built from `since` and a
                replacement. Used for aliases and enum members with `new_name`.
                `{old}` and `{new}` are replaced with the plain paths of the
                deprecated object and its replacement. `{new_link}` is a link to
                the replacement in code font. It only shows the name if the
                replacement is in the same module or enum. `{since}` is replaced
                with the version, as written. The result is rendered as Markdown.
                The notice appears next to the deprecated object, so it doesn't
                repeat its name.
            show_target: Whether to show an alias' value as its target, instead
                of the private name imported for type checkers.
        """
        super().__init__()
        self.kind = kind
        """The kind of the admonition added to the docstring."""
        self.title = title or ""
        """The title of the admonition added to the docstring."""
        self.label = label
        """The label added to deprecated objects."""
        self.alias_table_functions = frozenset(alias_table_functions)
        """The paths of the functions that create a `__getattr__` from an alias table."""
        self.alias_classes = frozenset(alias_classes)
        """The paths of the callables that create one alias entry."""
        self.member_wrapper_functions = frozenset(member_wrapper_functions)
        """The paths of the callables that wrap a deprecated enum member's value."""
        self.default_message = default_message
        """The template for notices built from `since` and a replacement."""
        self.show_target = show_target
        """Whether to show an alias' value as its target."""

    def on_module_members(self, *, mod: Module, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Mark every name in the module's alias table, if it has one.

        Args:
            mod: The module whose members were just collected.
            **kwargs: Other arguments passed by Griffe, not used.
        """
        call = self._alias_table_call(mod)
        if call is None:
            return
        for entry in self._alias_entries(mod, call):
            # Only `since` and the target affect the notice. `message` is for
            # the runtime warning, which is shown in a terminal.
            text, problem, fix = self._notice(
                f"{mod.path}.{entry.name}",
                entry.new,
                local=entry.local,
                since=entry.since,
                since_given=entry.since_given,
                unknown_since="because `since` can't be read",
                unknown_new="because the target can't be read",
            )

            member = mod.members.get(entry.name)
            if not isinstance(member, Attribute):
                # It isn't declared at all, or it's declared by an import like
                # `from new import New as Old` under `TYPE_CHECKING`.
                _logger.debug(
                    "%s.%s: the alias isn't declared as an attribute for type "
                    "checkers, adding one",
                    mod.path,
                    entry.name,
                )
                member = Attribute(entry.name, parent=mod)
                mod.set_member(entry.name, member)

            if self.show_target:
                if entry.new is None:
                    _logger.warning(
                        "%s.%s: the target of the alias can't be read, so its "
                        "value is shown as written",
                        mod.path,
                        entry.name,
                    )
                else:
                    member.value = ExprName(entry.new)
            self._mark(
                member, text, problem=problem, fix=fix, generic=problem is not None
            )

    # Aliases and enum members give different reasons for what they can't read,
    # so the caller has to pass them.
    def _notice(  # pylint: disable=too-many-arguments
        self,
        old: str,
        new: str | None,
        *,
        local: bool,
        since: str | None,
        since_given: bool,
        unknown_since: str,
        unknown_new: str,
    ) -> tuple[str, str | None, str]:
        """Build a notice from `since` and the replacement.

        If either argument is missing or can't be read, use a generic notice
        with the information we have.

        Args:
            old: The fully qualified path of the deprecated object.
            new: The fully qualified path of its replacement, or `None` if it
                can't be read.
            local: Whether the replacement is in the same module or enum.
                If so, the link only shows the replacement's name.
            since: The version the object is deprecated since, or `None` if it
                isn't given or can't be read.
            since_given: Whether `since` is passed. If not, the warning says
                so, and suggests passing it.
            unknown_since: The reason the version is unknown even though
                `since` is passed. Included in the warning if `since` is `None`.
            unknown_new: The reason the replacement is unknown. Included in the
                warning if `new` is `None`.

        Returns:
            The notice, why it's incomplete, or `None` if it's complete, and how
                to fix it. A notice is complete if it says everything the
                deprecations guide asks for.
        """
        fix = "Write a `Deprecated:` section in the docstring"
        link = None if new is None else _link(new, local=local)
        if since is not None and link is not None:
            try:
                # `since` is a value, not part of the template, so we insert
                # it as written, even if it has braces.
                return (
                    self.default_message.format(
                        old=old, new=new, new_link=link, since=since
                    ),
                    None,
                    fix,
                )
            except (AttributeError, IndexError, KeyError, ValueError):
                return (
                    _generic_message(since=since, new_link=link),
                    "the `default_message` option can only use {old}, {new}, "
                    "{new_link} and {since}, so a generic notice is shown",
                    fix,
                )
        missing = []
        if since is None:
            reason = unknown_since if since_given else "because `since` isn't given"
            missing.append(f"since which version it is deprecated, {reason}")
            if not since_given and link is not None:
                fix = "Pass `since` or write a `Deprecated:` section in the docstring"
        if link is None:
            missing.append(f"what to use instead, {unknown_new}")
        return (
            _generic_message(since=since, new_link=link),
            f"the notice can't say {', nor '.join(missing)}",
            fix,
        )

    def on_class_members(self, *, cls: Class, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Mark every wrapped enum member of the class, if it has any.

        Args:
            cls: The class whose members were just collected.
            **kwargs: Other arguments passed by Griffe, not used.
        """
        for member in cls.members.values():
            value = getattr(member, "value", None)
            if not isinstance(member, Attribute) or not isinstance(value, ExprCall):
                continue
            if value.canonical_path not in self.member_wrapper_functions:
                continue
            # Once an argument is unpacked, we can't tell which argument is
            # which. In `deprecated_member(*ARGS, "...")`, for example, the
            # first argument isn't necessarily the value. The member is still
            # deprecated, so we mark it, but we leave the call as written.
            if any(
                isinstance(argument, (ExprVarPositional, ExprVarKeyword))
                for argument in value.arguments
            ):
                _logger.warning(
                    "%s: the deprecation wrapper's arguments are unpacked, so "
                    "its value is shown as the whole call",
                    member.path,
                )
                self._mark(
                    member,
                    _generic_message(),
                    problem="the deprecation message can't be read, so a generic "
                    "notice is shown",
                    generic=True,
                )
                continue
            arguments = _wrapper_arguments(value)
            if arguments is None:
                # This call would fail at runtime, so it doesn't deprecate
                # anything.
                _logger.warning(
                    "%s: the deprecation wrapper's arguments don't match "
                    "`deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None, "
                    "since=None)`, which needs `message` or `new_name`, so the "
                    "member isn't marked",
                    member.path,
                )
                continue
            # Show the member's actual value, not the wrapper call, even if we
            # can't read the other arguments. We know the value either way.
            member.value = arguments.value
            self._mark_member(cls, member, arguments)

    def _mark_member(
        self, cls: Class, member: Attribute, arguments: _WrapperArguments
    ) -> None:
        """Mark a wrapped enum member using the information we can read.

        Args:
            cls: The enum the member belongs to.
            member: The member to mark.
            arguments: The arguments of its wrapper call.
        """
        since = None if arguments.since is None else _string(arguments.since)
        if arguments.since is not None and since is None:
            _logger.debug(
                "%s: `since` isn't a string literal, documenting what can be read",
                member.path,
            )
        new_name = None if arguments.new_name is None else _string(arguments.new_name)
        if arguments.new_name is not None and new_name is None:
            _logger.debug(
                "%s: `new_name` isn't a string literal, documenting what can be read",
                member.path,
            )
        message = None if arguments.message is None else _string(arguments.message)
        if new_name is not None or (arguments.new_name is not None and message is None):
            # As for aliases, `message` only changes the runtime warning. We
            # only show it if we can't read `new_name`, because then it's the
            # only thing that can say what to use instead.
            text, problem, fix = self._notice(
                member.path,
                None if new_name is None else f"{cls.path}.{new_name}",
                local=True,
                since=since,
                since_given=arguments.since is not None,
                unknown_since="because `since` isn't a string literal",
                unknown_new="because `new_name` isn't a string literal",
            )
            self._mark(
                member, text, problem=problem, fix=fix, generic=problem is not None
            )
            return
        if message is not None:
            # Without a readable `new_name`, only the runtime warning can tell
            # the reader what to use instead. Show it, even though it's for a
            # terminal. `since` isn't part of the warning, so we add the
            # version before it if we know it.
            self._mark(
                member,
                message if since is None else f"Deprecated since {since}. {message}",
                problem="there is no notice written for the documentation, "
                "so the runtime warning is shown instead",
            )
            return
        _logger.debug(
            "%s: the deprecation message isn't a string literal, so the "
            "member is marked with a generic notice",
            member.path,
        )
        self._mark(
            member,
            _generic_message(since=since),
            problem="the deprecation message isn't a string literal, so a "
            "generic notice is shown",
            generic=True,
        )

    def _alias_table_call(self, mod: Module) -> ExprCall | None:
        """Return the module's alias table call, if it has one.

        Args:
            mod: The module to look at.

        Returns:
            The call assigned to the module's `__getattr__`, or `None` if the
            module has no `__getattr__`, or if it isn't created by an alias
            table function.
        """
        value = getattr(mod.members.get("__getattr__"), "value", None)
        if isinstance(value, ExprCall) and value.canonical_path in (
            self.alias_table_functions
        ):
            return value
        return None

    def _alias_entries(self, mod: Module, call: ExprCall) -> list[_AliasEntry]:
        """Get the alias entries from an alias table call.

        The first positional argument is the module name, so it's skipped. Every
        other positional argument must be an alias entry call. Keyword arguments
        are ignored, because they can't be entries.

        Args:
            mod: The module where the call was found, used in log messages.
            call: The alias table call to read.

        Returns:
            Every entry whose name can be read, in the order they were written.
        """
        entries: list[_AliasEntry] = []
        module_seen = False
        for argument in call.arguments:
            if isinstance(argument, (ExprKeyword, ExprVarKeyword)):
                continue
            if isinstance(argument, ExprVarPositional):
                # Only `module` could be in there, so we stop skipping the first
                # argument. A module name is never an entry anyway.
                module_seen = True
                _logger.warning(
                    "%s: the alias entries in `%s` are unpacked, so they aren't "
                    "marked",
                    mod.path,
                    argument,
                )
                continue
            if not module_seen:
                module_seen = True
                continue
            entry = self._alias_entry(mod, argument)
            if entry is not None:
                entries.append(entry)
        return entries

    def _alias_entry(self, mod: Module, node: Any) -> _AliasEntry | None:
        """Read as much as possible from one alias entry.

        The extension only needs the name to mark the alias. The target and
        `since` are only read if they are string literals. The message is never
        read.

        Args:
            mod: The module where the entry was found, used in log messages.
            node: The expression passed as the entry.

        Returns:
            The information read from the entry. If the name can't be read, or the
                arguments don't match the ones of `DeprecatedAlias`, `None`.
        """
        if not (
            isinstance(node, ExprCall) and node.canonical_path in self.alias_classes
        ):
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the alias entry `%s` isn't a call to a known alias class, "
                "so it's skipped",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
            return None
        if any(isinstance(argument, ExprVarPositional) for argument in node.arguments):
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the arguments of the alias entry `%s` are unpacked, so "
                "it's skipped",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
            return None
        if any(isinstance(argument, ExprVarKeyword) for argument in node.arguments):
            return self._alias_entry_with_unpacked_keywords(mod, node)
        arguments = _alias_entry_arguments(node)
        if arguments is None:
            # This call would fail at runtime, so it doesn't deprecate anything.
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the alias entry `%s` needs a positional name, `new_module`, "
                "`new_name` or both, and only accepts `since` and `message` "
                "as extra arguments, so it's skipped",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
            return None
        name_node, *other_nodes = arguments
        name = _string(name_node)
        if name is None:
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the name of the alias entry `%s` isn't a string literal, so "
                "it's skipped",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
            return None
        # The message is only used for the runtime warning, so we never read it.
        new_module, new_name, since = (
            None if other is None else _string(other) for other in other_nodes[:3]
        )
        unreadable = [
            other is not None and value is None
            for other, value in zip(other_nodes, (new_module, new_name, since))
        ]
        if any(unreadable):
            _logger.debug(
                "%s: an argument of the alias entry `%s` isn't a string literal, "
                "so only the rest is documented",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
        # Like at runtime: without `new_module`, the object is still in this
        # module, and without `new_name`, it kept its name.
        new = (
            None
            if unreadable[0] or unreadable[1]
            else f"{new_module or mod.path}.{new_name or name}"
        )
        return _AliasEntry(
            name, new, new_module in (None, mod.path), since, other_nodes[2] is not None
        )

    def _alias_entry_with_unpacked_keywords(
        self, mod: Module, node: ExprCall
    ) -> _AliasEntry | None:
        """Read the name of an alias entry with unpacked keyword arguments.

        Any keyword argument could be in the `**kwargs`, so the extension can only
        read the name.

        Args:
            mod: The module where the entry was found, used in log messages.
            node: The entry call.

        Returns:
            The entry with only its name, or `None` if the name can't be read.
        """
        positional = [
            argument
            for argument in node.arguments
            if not isinstance(argument, (ExprKeyword, ExprVarKeyword))
        ]
        name = _literal(positional[0]) if len(positional) == 1 else None
        if not isinstance(name, str):
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the arguments of the alias entry `%s` are unpacked, so "
                "it's skipped",
                mod.path,
                node,
            )
            return None
        _logger.debug(
            "%s: the keyword arguments of the alias entry `%s` are unpacked, so "
            "only its name is documented",
            mod.path,
            node,
        )
        return _AliasEntry(name, None, False, None, True)

    def _mark(
        self,
        member: Attribute,
        text: str,
        *,
        problem: str | None = None,
        fix: str = "Write a `Deprecated:` section in the docstring",
        generic: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        """Mark one member as deprecated and add its notice.

        If the docstring has a hand-written notice, it's used instead of `text`.
        It's also moved to the top of the docstring, where a generated notice
        would go.

        Args:
            member: The member to mark.
            text: The notice.
            problem: Why the notice is incomplete, if it is. It's logged as a
                warning, unless there is a hand-written notice.
            fix: How to fix the problem, added to the warning.
            generic: Whether `text` is the generic notice. If it is, and another
                extension already set a message, that message is used instead,
                also as the notice.
        """
        if generic and isinstance(member.deprecated, str):
            # Another extension could read the message, so we show that one,
            # and nothing is missing from the docs.
            text, problem = member.deprecated, None
        member.deprecated = text
        if self.label:
            member.labels.add(self.label)
        if member.docstring is None:
            member.docstring = Docstring("", parent=member)
        sections = member.docstring.parsed
        written = self._handwritten_notice(sections)
        if written is not None:
            # A docstring must start with its summary, so the hand-written notice
            # can't be at the top in the source. We move it there, so it's in the
            # same place as the generated notices.
            sections.insert(0, sections.pop(written))
            return
        if problem is not None:
            # The documentation says less than the guide asks for, so a strict
            # build should fail.
            _logger.warning("%s: %s. %s to fix this.", member.path, problem, fix)
        sections.insert(
            0,
            DocstringSectionAdmonition(kind=self.kind, text=text, title=self.title),
        )

    def _handwritten_notice(self, sections: list[DocstringSection]) -> int | None:
        """Find a hand-written deprecation notice in a docstring.

        A hand-written notice is a `Deprecated` section, or an admonition with the
        same title as the ones this extension adds (case-insensitive).

        Args:
            sections: The parsed sections of the docstring.

        Returns:
            The index of the first hand-written notice, or `None` if there is
                none.
        """
        for index, section in enumerate(sections):
            if section.kind is DocstringSectionKind.deprecated:
                return index
            if (
                section.kind is DocstringSectionKind.admonition
                and str(getattr(section, "title", "")).strip().lower()
                == self.title.strip().lower()
            ):
                return index
        return None

Initialize the extension.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION kind

The kind of the admonition added to the docstring.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'danger'

title

The title of that admonition. If empty, the admonition has no title.

TYPE: str | None DEFAULT: 'Deprecated'

label

The label added to deprecated objects, or None to add no label.

TYPE: str | None DEFAULT: 'deprecated'

alias_table_functions

The fully qualified paths of the functions that create a module __getattr__ from an alias table. Their calls are read as if they were calls to deprecated_aliases(module, /, *aliases): every positional argument after the module is an alias entry, and keyword arguments are ignored.

TYPE: Sequence[str] DEFAULT: ('frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases',)

alias_classes

The fully qualified paths of the callables that create one alias entry. Their calls are read as if they were calls to DeprecatedAlias(name, /, *, new_module=None, new_name=None, since=None, message=None), with at least one of new_module and new_name. since and message are optional and independent.

TYPE: Sequence[str] DEFAULT: ('frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias',)

member_wrapper_functions

The fully qualified paths of the callables that wrap an enum member's value to deprecate it. They can be classes or functions, because calling them looks the same. Their calls are read as if they were calls to deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None, since=None). At least one of message and new_name is required.

TYPE: Sequence[str] DEFAULT: ('frequenz.core.enum.deprecated_member', 'frequenz.core.enum.DeprecatedMember')

default_message

The template for notices built from since and a replacement. Used for aliases and enum members with new_name. {old} and {new} are replaced with the plain paths of the deprecated object and its replacement. {new_link} is a link to the replacement in code font. It only shows the name if the replacement is in the same module or enum. {since} is replaced with the version, as written. The result is rendered as Markdown. The notice appears next to the deprecated object, so it doesn't repeat its name.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'Deprecated since {since}. Use {new_link} instead.'

show_target

Whether to show an alias' value as its target, instead of the private name imported for type checkers.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

def __init__(  # pylint: disable=too-many-arguments
    self,
    kind: str = "danger",
    title: str | None = "Deprecated",
    label: str | None = "deprecated",
    *,
    alias_table_functions: Sequence[str] = (
        "frequenz.core.warnings.deprecated_aliases",
    ),
    alias_classes: Sequence[str] = ("frequenz.core.warnings.DeprecatedAlias",),
    member_wrapper_functions: Sequence[str] = (
        "frequenz.core.enum.deprecated_member",
        "frequenz.core.enum.DeprecatedMember",
    ),
    default_message: str = "Deprecated since {since}. Use {new_link} instead.",
    show_target: bool = True,
) -> None:
    """Initialize the extension.

    Args:
        kind: The kind of the admonition added to the docstring.
        title: The title of that admonition. If empty, the admonition has no
            title.
        label: The label added to deprecated objects, or `None` to add no
            label.
        alias_table_functions: The fully qualified paths of the functions that
            create a module `__getattr__` from an alias table. Their calls are
            read as if they were calls to
            `deprecated_aliases(module, /, *aliases)`: every positional
            argument after the module is an alias entry, and keyword
            arguments are ignored.
        alias_classes: The fully qualified paths of the callables that create
            one alias entry. Their calls are read as if they were calls to
            `DeprecatedAlias(name, /, *, new_module=None, new_name=None,
            since=None, message=None)`, with at least one of `new_module` and
            `new_name`. `since` and `message` are optional and independent.
        member_wrapper_functions: The fully qualified paths of the callables
            that wrap an enum member's value to deprecate it. They can be
            classes or functions, because calling them looks the same. Their
            calls are read as if they were calls to
            `deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None,
            since=None)`. At least one of `message` and `new_name` is required.
        default_message: The template for notices built from `since` and a
            replacement. Used for aliases and enum members with `new_name`.
            `{old}` and `{new}` are replaced with the plain paths of the
            deprecated object and its replacement. `{new_link}` is a link to
            the replacement in code font. It only shows the name if the
            replacement is in the same module or enum. `{since}` is replaced
            with the version, as written. The result is rendered as Markdown.
            The notice appears next to the deprecated object, so it doesn't
            repeat its name.
        show_target: Whether to show an alias' value as its target, instead
            of the private name imported for type checkers.
    """
    super().__init__()
    self.kind = kind
    """The kind of the admonition added to the docstring."""
    self.title = title or ""
    """The title of the admonition added to the docstring."""
    self.label = label
    """The label added to deprecated objects."""
    self.alias_table_functions = frozenset(alias_table_functions)
    """The paths of the functions that create a `__getattr__` from an alias table."""
    self.alias_classes = frozenset(alias_classes)
    """The paths of the callables that create one alias entry."""
    self.member_wrapper_functions = frozenset(member_wrapper_functions)
    """The paths of the callables that wrap a deprecated enum member's value."""
    self.default_message = default_message
    """The template for notices built from `since` and a replacement."""
    self.show_target = show_target
    """Whether to show an alias' value as its target."""

def on_class_members(self, *, cls: Class, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Mark every wrapped enum member of the class, if it has any.

    Args:
        cls: The class whose members were just collected.
        **kwargs: Other arguments passed by Griffe, not used.
    """
    for member in cls.members.values():
        value = getattr(member, "value", None)
        if not isinstance(member, Attribute) or not isinstance(value, ExprCall):
            continue
        if value.canonical_path not in self.member_wrapper_functions:
            continue
        # Once an argument is unpacked, we can't tell which argument is
        # which. In `deprecated_member(*ARGS, "...")`, for example, the
        # first argument isn't necessarily the value. The member is still
        # deprecated, so we mark it, but we leave the call as written.
        if any(
            isinstance(argument, (ExprVarPositional, ExprVarKeyword))
            for argument in value.arguments
        ):
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the deprecation wrapper's arguments are unpacked, so "
                "its value is shown as the whole call",
                member.path,
            )
            self._mark(
                member,
                _generic_message(),
                problem="the deprecation message can't be read, so a generic "
                "notice is shown",
                generic=True,
            )
            continue
        arguments = _wrapper_arguments(value)
        if arguments is None:
            # This call would fail at runtime, so it doesn't deprecate
            # anything.
            _logger.warning(
                "%s: the deprecation wrapper's arguments don't match "
                "`deprecated_member(value, message=None, *, new_name=None, "
                "since=None)`, which needs `message` or `new_name`, so the "
                "member isn't marked",
                member.path,
            )
            continue
        # Show the member's actual value, not the wrapper call, even if we
        # can't read the other arguments. We know the value either way.
        member.value = arguments.value
        self._mark_member(cls, member, arguments)

def on_module_members(self, *, mod: Module, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Mark every name in the module's alias table, if it has one.

    Args:
        mod: The module whose members were just collected.
        **kwargs: Other arguments passed by Griffe, not used.
    """
    call = self._alias_table_call(mod)
    if call is None:
        return
    for entry in self._alias_entries(mod, call):
        # Only `since` and the target affect the notice. `message` is for
        # the runtime warning, which is shown in a terminal.
        text, problem, fix = self._notice(
            f"{mod.path}.{entry.name}",
            entry.new,
            local=entry.local,
            since=entry.since,
            since_given=entry.since_given,
            unknown_since="because `since` can't be read",
            unknown_new="because the target can't be read",
        )

        member = mod.members.get(entry.name)
        if not isinstance(member, Attribute):
            # It isn't declared at all, or it's declared by an import like
            # `from new import New as Old` under `TYPE_CHECKING`.
            _logger.debug(
                "%s.%s: the alias isn't declared as an attribute for type "
                "checkers, adding one",
                mod.path,
                entry.name,
            )
            member = Attribute(entry.name, parent=mod)
            mod.set_member(entry.name, member)

        if self.show_target:
            if entry.new is None:
                _logger.warning(
                    "%s.%s: the target of the alias can't be read, so its "
                    "value is shown as written",
                    mod.path,
                    entry.name,
                )
            else:
                member.value = ExprName(entry.new)
        self._mark(
            member, text, problem=problem, fix=fix, generic=problem is not None
        )
